title: Geologic and Hydrometeorological Processes
seo_title: Grade 11 General Science: Geologic and Hydrometeorological Processes Worksheets
standard_code: Grade 11 General Science, Term 3: Earth and space science
standard_text: Geologic and hydrometeorological processes that shape the Philippines: plate movement, earthquakes and volcanism; weathering, erosion and mass wasting; typhoons, monsoons, floods and the water cycle. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 3)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 3): plate movement, earthquakes, volcanoes, weathering and landslides, typhoons, monsoons and floods. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Geologic processes come from inside the Earth; hydrometeorological ones from weather and water.
body_html:
How to think about it

Geologic processes are driven by the Earth's internal heat: plates move, faults slip and cause earthquakes, and magma rises to form volcanoes such as Mayon and Taal. Over long times these processes build mountains and islands.

Hydrometeorological processes are driven by the Sun's energy: typhoons, monsoon rains (habagat and amihan), floods, and the water cycle. Weathering, erosion and landslides wear the land down, especially on steep, deforested slopes after heavy rain.

Example

Is a landslide after heavy rain a geologic or hydrometeorological process?

Triggered by rain

Answer: hydrometeorological (rain-triggered mass wasting)

Example

What drives plate movement?

Inside the Earth

Answer: mantle convection

Common mistakes

  • Thinking typhoons cause earthquakes.
  • Thinking volcanoes only destroy.
  • Thinking floods happen only during typhoons.

faq.q: Why are landslides common in the Cordillera?
faq.a: The slopes are steep and receive heavy rain.

faq.q: How does the habagat bring floods?
faq.a: It brings days of heavy rain that fill rivers.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms Iceland splitting slowly apart?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: sudden earthquakes along a fault line
fold mountains such as the Himalayas
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): fold mountains such as the Himalayas.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the layer of liquid iron and nickel?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a divergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: divergent (plates move apart): mid-ocean ridges.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the thin, solid outer layer we live on?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: convergent (plates move together): the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): volcanoes along the Andes.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): the Alpine Fault in New Zealand.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a divergent boundary?
c: fold mountains such as the Himalayas
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
sudden earthquakes along a fault line
items.e: divergent (plates move apart): Iceland splitting slowly apart.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the solid center of iron and nickel?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: What is Earth's outer core like?
c: the solid center of iron and nickel
the layer of liquid iron and nickel
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: What is Earth's inner core like?
c: the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
the solid center of iron and nickel
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the layer of liquid iron and nickel
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Mark uses a jigsaw of continents to show Gondwana. What is a limitation of his model?
c: It shows plates moving too slowly.
Coastlines have changed, and the real fit uses the edges of the continental shelves.
items.e: Models simplify reality.

items.q: What is Earth's mantle like?
c: the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the layer of liquid iron and nickel
the solid center of iron and nickel
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Why do scientists keep revising the theory of plate tectonics?
c: New evidence from GPS, sea-floor mapping and earthquakes improves it.
items.e: Scientific theories develop with new evidence.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms sudden earthquakes along a fault line?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: What is Earth's crust like?
c: the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the layer of liquid iron and nickel
the solid center of iron and nickel
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms new sea floor?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Isabel models convection by heating water with food coloring. What does the moving color represent?
items.e: Warm material rises and cool material sinks.

items.q: Which waves usually cause the most damage in an earthquake?
items.e: They have large amplitudes and travel along the surface.

items.q: What is the epicenter of an earthquake?
c: the deepest point of the Earth
a place far from the earthquake
the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus
items.e: Shaking is usually strongest near the epicenter.

items.q: What causes a tsunami?
c: a sudden movement of the sea floor, usually from a large undersea earthquake, which displaces water
items.e: Landslides and volcanoes can also cause them.

items.q: At Kristine's station, S waves arrive 60 s after P waves. Using the rule of thumb of 8 km per second of lag, how far away was the earthquake?
At Dennis's station, S waves arrive 10 s after P waves. Using the rule of thumb of 8 km per second of lag, how far away was the earthquake?
At Kenneth's station, S waves arrive 90 s after P waves. Using the rule of thumb of 8 km per second of lag, how far away was the earthquake?
What should you do during an earthquake?
c: run outside while the ground is shaking
items.e: Drop down, cover your head under a sturdy table and hold on.

items.q: Which agency gives earthquake information in the Philippines?
items.e: PHIVOLCS reports magnitude and intensity.

items.q: What can trigger a landslide?
c: heavy rain, earthquakes or removal of vegetation on steep slopes
items.e: Thredbo (1997) was a landslide disaster.

items.q: What does the intensity of an earthquake describe?
c: how strongly it is felt and the damage it causes at a place
items.e: Intensity is different in different places; PHIVOLCS uses intensities I to X.

items.q: What is the focus of an earthquake?
c: the point on the surface above it
the point inside the Earth where the rocks first break
the place where the tsunami hits
items.e: The focus is also called the hypocenter.

items.q: At Jasmine's station, S waves arrive 5 s after P waves. Using the rule of thumb of 8 km per second of lag, how far away was the earthquake?
Which type of volcano has gentle slopes and runny basalt lava?
items.e: Hawaii's volcanoes are shield volcanoes.

items.q: Why do tsunamis become taller as they reach the coast?
c: the wave slows in shallow water, so the water piles up
they gain energy from the beach
items.e: Their speed is about √(gd).

items.q: What causes most earthquakes?
c: sudden movement of rocks along faults in the Earth's crust
items.e: Energy is released as seismic waves.

items.q: Which is a way to reduce the risk of earthquake damage?
c: building codes that require flexible, reinforced structures
items.e: Planning and drills also help.

items.q: What is the difference between hazard and risk?
c: a hazard is always a disaster
a hazard is a possible source of harm; risk combines how likely it is and how severe the consequences are
risk is the cause and hazard is the result
items.e: Risk = likelihood × consequence.

items.q: An earthquake is 600 km from a seismograph. Using about 8 km per second of S–P lag, how long after the P waves do the S waves arrive?
About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 7 earthquake than a magnitude 4 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
What causes most earthquakes?
c: sudden movement along faults as stress built up between plates is released
items.e: The point of rupture is the focus.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 60 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicenter?
items.e: 60 × 8 = 480 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicenter.

items.q: A community plans hurricane-rated roofs and storm shutters. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: Which volcano erupted in 1991 in one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century?
items.e: Ash from Pinatubo cooled the whole Earth slightly for about two years.

items.q: What is magma called when it reaches the surface?
items.e: Magma is molten rock underground; lava is molten rock on the surface.

items.q: Which signs can warn that a volcano may erupt?
c: small earthquakes, ground swelling and more gas emissions
items.e: Monitoring reduces deaths.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 20 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicenter?
items.e: 20 × 8 = 160 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicenter.

items.q: Which volcano lies on an island in a lake in Batangas?
items.e: Taal Volcano is inside Taal Lake.

items.q: What is a pyroclastic flow?
c: a fast, very hot flow of gas, ash and rock down a volcano's slope
a slow stream of clean water
items.e: Pyroclastic flows are among the most dangerous volcanic hazards.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from volcanic eruptions?
c: drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
clearing brush to make defensible space around homes
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 30 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicenter?
items.e: 30 × 8 = 240 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicenter.

items.q: A community plans monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 7 earthquake than a magnitude 5 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(7 − 5) = 100 times.

items.q: Which Philippine volcano is famous for its almost perfect cone shape?
items.e: Mayon is a stratovolcano with a nearly perfect cone.

items.q: How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 9.1 earthquake than a magnitude 6.5 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(9.1 − 6.5) = 398 times.

items.q: What is an active volcano?
c: a mountain with no magma at all
a volcano that has erupted in historical times or shows signs of activity
a volcano that will never erupt again
items.e: An inactive volcano has not erupted for a very long time.

items.q: What does a higher Volcano Alert Level mean?
c: a greater chance of a dangerous eruption
items.e: Alert levels go from 0 (normal) to 5 (hazardous eruption in progress).

items.q: A tsunami crosses ocean 5,000 m deep. Its speed is v = √(gd). How long does it take to travel 4,000 km? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Why did the 1989 Newcastle earthquake cause so much damage despite a magnitude of only 5.6?
c: it was shallow and close to a city, and some buildings were on soft sediments that amplified shaking
it was far from the city
items.e: Thirteen people died.

items.q: A tsunami crosses ocean 1,000 m deep. Its speed is v = √(gd). How long does it take to travel 2,000 km? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
What is a lahar?
c: a mudflow of volcanic ash and water, often after heavy rain
items.e: Lahars from Pinatubo buried towns for years after the eruption.

items.q: Iron in rocks reacts with water and oxygen and turns red-brown. Which type of weathering is this?
items.e: Physical weathering breaks rock into pieces; chemical weathering changes the minerals.

items.q: Why are the Earth's resources such as metal ores limited?
c: They are made again every year.
They took millions of years to form and are being used much faster.
items.e: Finite resources.

items.q: A rock in a desert heats up by day and cools at night until its surface peels. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: Plant roots grow into cracks and split the rock. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: A mountain range rises 4 mm per year. How much higher would it be after 5,000,000 years (ignoring erosion)? (1 km = 1,000,000 mm)
Why are pebbles on a beach rounded?
c: They have been rolled and knocked against each other by water.
items.e: Erosion.

items.q: Water gets into a crack, freezes and expands, and the crack gets wider. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: A river cuts down into rock 0.2 mm per year. How deep will its canyon be after 5,000,000 years? (1 m = 1,000 mm)
What is a disadvantage of solar and wind power?
c: their output varies with weather and time of day, so storage or backup is needed
items.e: Batteries and pumped hydro store energy.

items.q: Burrowing animals break up rock near the surface. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: What is an artesian aquifer?
c: a confined aquifer in which pressure pushes water up a bore without pumping
items.e: It is trapped between impermeable layers.

items.q: What does the rock cycle show?
c: how rocks are made in one day
how rocks change from one type to another over very long times
items.e: Driven by heat and weather.

items.q: Rainwater with CO₂ dissolves a marble statue. Which type of weathering is this?
items.e: Physical weathering breaks rock into pieces; chemical weathering changes the minerals.

items.q: A mountain range rises 10 mm per year. How much higher would it be after 500,000 years (ignoring erosion)? (1 km = 1,000,000 mm)
Feldspar in granite slowly changes into clay in wet soil. Which type of weathering is this?
items.e: Physical weathering breaks rock into pieces; chemical weathering changes the minerals.

items.q: Why is recycling aluminum better than mining new ore?
c: It saves ore and uses much less energy.
items.e: Conserve resources.

items.q: Acid rain damages a marble statue. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: Rainwater, which is slightly acidic, slowly dissolves limestone. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: A river erodes downward 0.2 mm per year. About how long would it take to cut a canyon 100 m deep?
A mountain range rises 5 mm per year. How much higher would it be after 1,000,000 years (ignoring erosion)? (1 km = 1,000,000 mm)
Which is the correct order as a storm grows stronger?
c: tropical depression → tropical storm → severe tropical storm → typhoon → super typhoon
items.e: PAGASA classifies tropical cyclones by wind speed.

items.q: Which statement about La Niña is correct?
c: it can bring more rain and stronger storms to the Philippines
items.e: La Niña is the opposite of El Niño.

items.q: How does heat move through the mantle?
c: mostly by convection: hot rock slowly rises and cooler rock sinks
items.e: Convection takes millions of years.

items.q: Why should families near rivers evacuate during a strong typhoon?
c: heavy rain can cause floods and flash floods
items.e: Heavy rain raises river levels quickly.

items.q: What should people prepare for in the rainy season?
items.e: Clean drains and prepare go bags.

items.q: Hazel fills a 400 mL beaker with dry sediment, then adds 100 mL of water until it reaches the top of the sediment. What is the porosity?
Why does the Earth's tilt matter for seasons?
c: the part tilted toward the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days
the tilted part is closer to the Moon
items.e: Direct sunlight heats the surface more.

items.q: Diane fills a 400 mL beaker with dry sediment, then adds 140 mL of water until it reaches the top of the sediment. What is the porosity?
Water expands by about 9% when it freezes. 250 mL of water freezes in a rock crack. About what volume does the ice take up?
What is the habagat?
c: the southwest monsoon, a warm, moist wind that brings heavy rain
items.e: It blows from about June to September.

items.q: A student freezes 80 mL of water in a plastic cup. By about how much does the volume increase? (Water expands about 9% when it freezes.)
A student freezes 300 mL of water in a plastic cup. By about how much does the volume increase? (Water expands about 9% when it freezes.)
Mae fills a 100 mL beaker with dry sediment, then adds 40 mL of water until it reaches the top of the sediment. What is the porosity?
What is a storm surge?
c: a wave made by a ship
an abnormal rise of sea water pushed onto land by a typhoon's winds
items.e: Storm surges can flood coastal areas, as in Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in 2013.

items.q: Which statement about El Niño is correct?
c: it can bring less rain and drought to the Philippines
it makes the Earth stop rotating
items.e: During El Niño, rain is often below normal.

items.q: Which item should be in an emergency go bag?
c: a flashlight, water, food, medicine and a radio
items.e: A go bag helps a family survive the first days after a disaster.

items.q: Lance fills a 100 mL beaker with dry sediment, then adds 20 mL of water until it reaches the top of the sediment. What is the porosity?
What is a low pressure area (LPA)?
c: a place with very cold air
a region where air pressure is lower than around it, which may develop into a tropical cyclone
items.e: Air rises in an LPA and clouds form.

items.q: Why are many typhoons given local names by PAGASA?
c: because each one has a different eye
so that people can easily identify and remember each storm
items.e: Local names help people follow warnings.

items.q: What is the amihan?
c: the northeast monsoon, a cooler, drier wind from about November to February
items.e: Amihan brings cooler weather to Luzon.
